sectionTitle: Four things I built, and why they were hard.

items.title: University of Dayton Magazine
items.problem: A university magazine publishing on a CMS with no component model, where every new issue quietly drifted away from the last one.
items.built: The content architecture, the issue template and the publishing path behind seven consecutive issues — plus most of the photography inside them.
items.outcome: Seven issues published and still live, from Winter 2023–24 through Summer 2025.

caseStudySections.title: Context
body: The University of Dayton Magazine publishes a few times a year to an audience of alumni, staff and prospective students. It runs on Cascade CMS — an enterprise system built around templates and structured data blocks rather than components.

Each issue had historically been assembled by hand. That works once. Across seven issues it produces seven subtly different magazines: headings that shift a few pixels, image crops that change ratio, navigation that behaves differently on a phone depending on which issue you landed in.

caseStudySections.title: Challenge
body: Cascade has no notion of a reusable component in the way a modern framework does. There is no import, no props, no composition. What it has is templates, regions, and structured data definitions — and non-technical editors who need to publish without touching any of it.
So the constraint was: produce component-like consistency using a system that has no components, for people who will never open a code editor.
caseStudySections.callout: The hard part was never the markup. It was designing a system that stays consistent when the person using it does not know it is a system.

caseStudySections.title: Approach
body: I treated the issue itself as the unit. One issue template, one structured data definition describing what an issue *is* — cover image, feature articles, departments, credits — and every page in an issue rendered from that.

Anything an editor could get wrong, I removed from their hands. Image ratios became fixed by the template rather than chosen at upload. Heading levels were emitted by the template, so the document outline could not be broken by someone bolding a line of text.
Where a choice genuinely belonged to the editor, it became an explicit field with a constrained set of options, not a free-text box.

caseStudySections.title: Architecture
body: Editors work only in the middle column. They never see the template layer, and the publish step is the same three clicks for every issue.

caseStudySections.title: Engineering
body: Semantic HTML with a single document outline per page, so the magazine reads correctly in a screen reader and in a search index.
CSS built on a small set of layout primitives rather than per-issue stylesheets — a feature spread and a department page differ by class, not by file.
Responsive images driven from the template so that a photograph uploaded once serves correctly on a phone and on a desktop.
Accessibility checked to WCAG AA: contrast, focus order, alt text enforced as a required field rather than an optional one.
GA4 wired in per issue so we could see which features were actually read.

caseStudySections.title: Result
body: Seven consecutive issues, from Winter 2023–24 through Summer 2025, all live and all built from the same template.
Publishing a new issue stopped being a project and became a task. A large share of the photography in those issues is mine, shot on campus across two years of weather.

caseStudySections.title: Reflection
body: I would push harder on the preview loop. Editors still discovered layout problems after publishing rather than before, because Cascade's preview does not faithfully represent the responsive output. A lightweight standalone preview — even a static page fed by the same structured data — would have caught most of it.

I would also instrument the template itself. I know which articles people read; I do not know which template regions editors struggled with, and that is the data that would have improved the system fastest.

items.title: The academic site programme
items.problem: Departments across the university each needed a site. Left alone, that produces a hundred inconsistent, inaccessible, unmaintained websites.
items.built: The shared templates, content workflows and release QA that the sites were built and published through, working inside an eight-person team.
items.outcome: 175+ academic and magazine sites shipped, with responsive, accessibility, cross-browser and production QA run before and after every release.

detail.label: Templating
detail.text: Pre-defined Cascade templates and custom WordPress themes and plugins, so a new department site starts from a known-good baseline instead of a blank page.

detail.label: Design handoff
detail.text: Figma wireframes and annotated prototypes handed off to responsive HTML/CSS/JS builds — I worked both sides of that handoff.

detail.label: Quality gate
detail.text: Responsive, functional, accessibility, browser and production QA performed before and after each release.

detail.label: Measurement
detail.text: GA4 and Qualtrics wired into pages so content decisions were made against real engagement data rather than opinion.

items.title: The image pipeline
items.kicker: Python and OpenCV, doing the boring half
items.problem: Every campus photograph was hand-corrected before publishing — exposure, colour, crop, resize — once per image, per person, forever.
items.built: A Python and OpenCV pipeline that normalises exposure and colour, tone-maps bracketed exposures, crops content-aware to each required ratio, and emits the responsive sizes the CMS needs.
items.outcome: Cut manual editing time by roughly 40% and made the look of campus photography consistent across cameras, photographers and lighting conditions.

stages.title: Ingest
stages.text: Read the shoot, normalise colour space, strip what should not be published.

stages.title: Normalise
stages.text: Exposure and white-balance correction so a gym, a snowstorm and a lecture hall end up in the same tonal family.

stages.title: Tone-map
stages.text: HDR tone mapping on bracketed sets — hold the highlight in a window without crushing the room.

stages.title: Frame
stages.text: Content-aware crop to every ratio the template needs, anchored so subjects survive the crop.

stages.title: Emit
stages.text: Dynamic resizing into the responsive ladder, named and shaped for the CMS to pick up.

caseStudySections.title: Context
body: A university publishes a great deal of photography: events, campus, sport, portraits, seasons. It arrives from several cameras, several photographers and wildly inconsistent light — a February snowstorm at noon and a basketball arena at night are not the same photographic problem.

Before it can go on a page, each frame gets corrected, cropped to whatever ratios the layout needs, and exported at several sizes. Done by hand, that is a few minutes per image. Multiply by an event shoot.

caseStudySections.title: Challenge
body: Three things made this harder than a batch-resize script.
First, correction is not a single transform. The right exposure adjustment for an arena is wrong for a snow scene; a fixed curve makes half the library worse.
Second, cropping is where naive automation fails most visibly. A centre crop to a 21:9 banner reliably removes people's heads. A crop is only acceptable if it knows where the subject is.
Third, the output had to drop into an existing CMS convention. A pipeline that produces beautiful files the publishing system cannot find is not a pipeline.
caseStudySections.callout: Automation that is right 90% of the time is worse than no automation, because someone now has to check 100% of it to find the 10%.

caseStudySections.title: Approach
body: I split correction from framing, and made both measurable rather than aesthetic.

Correction works off the image's own histogram: normalise exposure and white balance toward a target the whole library shares, so consistency is a property of the pipeline rather than of the photographer's mood that afternoon. Bracketed sets go through HDR tone mapping instead of being flattened.

Framing is content-aware. The crop window is chosen from where the visual content actually is, not from the geometric centre, then anchored so that the subject survives every ratio the template asks for.
And the pipeline is not permitted to be the last word. It writes derivatives alongside the original and never over it, so a bad automated decision costs one re-run, not one photograph.

caseStudySections.title: Architecture
body: Every stage is independent and re-runnable. Originals are immutable; everything downstream is a derivative that can be thrown away and regenerated.

caseStudySections.title: Engineering
body: Python and OpenCV throughout, with NumPy doing the array work — histogram analysis for exposure and white-balance normalisation, tone mapping for bracketed exposures, and content-aware crop-window selection for framing.
Dynamic resizing produces the responsive ladder in one pass rather than per-size re-decoding, which is where a naive implementation spends most of its time.
Output naming follows the CMS convention exactly, so publishing needs no manual step between the pipeline and the page.
The same discipline runs this portfolio: optimize_images.py in this repository is the small, public descendant of that pipeline.

caseStudySections.title: Result
body: Manual editing time fell by roughly 40%.
The less measurable result mattered more: campus photography started to look like it came from one publication instead of eleven different afternoons.

caseStudySections.title: Reflection
body: The content-aware crop is the part I would rebuild. It reasons about visual content generally; it should reason about people specifically, because people are what the crop destroys. A face and body detector gating the crop window would remove nearly every remaining failure case.

I would also keep a rejection log. I know how much time the pipeline saved. I do not know which images humans overrode afterwards, and that log is exactly the training signal needed to make the next version better.

items.title: Archive triage
items.kicker: Deciding what to delete, and proving it
items.problem: Over 2,500 digital magazine pages had accumulated across years of publishing, and nobody could say which of them were still worth keeping.
items.built: A computer-vision and analytics pipeline that scored every page for relevance — layout, text density, visual freshness, real usage — and produced a ranked retirement list with a full audit trail behind every recommendation.
items.outcome: 1,600+ obsolete pages and assets retired under university archival policy, every removal documented and reviewable.

splitPoints.label: Signal 1 — Layout
splitPoints.text: Page structure, analysed visually. Old templates look old; that is a measurable property of the rendered page, not a guess.

splitPoints.label: Signal 2 — Text density
splitPoints.text: How much substance the page actually carries, distinguishing a real article from an orphaned index or a stub.

splitPoints.label: Signal 3 — Visual freshness
splitPoints.text: Image classification across the page's media, flagging redundant, superseded or low-utility photographs.

splitPoints.label: Signal 4 — Usage
splitPoints.text: Real traffic and usage metrics, because a visually dated page that people still read is not obsolete.

splitPoints.label: The gate
splitPoints.text: Nothing was deleted by the pipeline. It ranked and recommended; a human approved. Deletion under archival policy is irreversible, so the system was built to never be the last word.

splitPoints.label: The record
splitPoints.text: Every processing step and content action written to structured audit reports, so any individual removal could be explained months later to the people accountable for the archive.

caseStudySections.title: Context
body: Years of magazine publishing leaves sediment. Over 2,500 digital pages had accumulated — feature articles, department pages, issue indexes, orphaned drafts, and a great deal of photography attached to all of it.
Some of it was still read. Some of it had not been visited in years. Nobody could tell you which was which without opening pages one at a time, and nobody had time to open 2,500 pages.

caseStudySections.title: Challenge
body: 'Obsolete' is not a property you can read off a page. It is a judgement combining how the page looks, what it contains, and whether anyone wants it — three signals that live in three different places.

And the stakes were asymmetric. Under university archival policy, removal is irreversible. A false positive destroys something a person is accountable for; a false negative costs a few kilobytes. Those are not remotely equal errors, and the system had to be designed around that asymmetry rather than around accuracy.
caseStudySections.callout: When one kind of mistake is permanent and the other is cheap, the correct system is not the most accurate one. It is the one that refuses to act alone.

caseStudySections.title: Approach
body: I made the pipeline an advisor, never an actor. It reads, scores, ranks and explains. A human decides.

Relevance was scored from four independent signals — page layout, text density, visual freshness of the attached media, and actual usage — precisely so that no single weak signal could condemn a page on its own. A dated-looking page that people still read scores as keep. That is the case the whole design exists to protect.
Everything the pipeline did was written down as it happened, not reconstructed afterwards.

caseStudySections.title: Architecture
body: Four signals in, one ranked recommendation out, a human gate before anything is touched, and an audit record written at every step.

caseStudySections.title: Engineering
body: OpenCV and TensorFlow for the visual side: scanning rendered pages to analyse layout structure and text density, and image classification across the attached media to detect redundant or superseded photographs.
Usage metrics joined against the visual scores, so the ranking reflected both what a page was and whether anyone wanted it.

Structured audit reporting as a first-class output rather than an afterthought — every processing step and every content action logged, and progress reported to department heads in a form they could actually review.

caseStudySections.title: Result
body: More than 1,600 obsolete magazines, pages and assets were retired, each one traceable to the evidence that justified it.
The archive got smaller and the parts people actually use got easier to find. Nothing was lost that anyone came looking for.

caseStudySections.title: Reflection
body: The scoring weights were set by judgement and tuned by inspection. With the review decisions captured as labels, the weights should have been learned from the humans overriding them — the review queue was a training set and I used it as a spreadsheet.

I would also have made the recommendations reversible for a fixed window rather than routing straight to permanent deletion. A thirty-day quarantine would have turned the most expensive possible error into an inconvenience, and would have let the system act far more confidently.
